going the course of sprouts through which aU pledges must pass before they finaUy

It so happened that this young pledge was not particularly weighed down with
cash of the realm, but the problem was eased to a degree when an upperclassman, who

Psi U took over, impressing the editors with his competence, his ability to write a
story. NaturaUy, being paid by the column inch for his writing, he was dUigent and

Upon graduating, he was able to pass along his responsibUities to another Brother.

porter.

recognized as ranking in the upper echelon of trial lawyers
in his city.
Moreover he discovered that several of the judges also were Psi U's and that they

up to an
ever-expanding experience for our young Brother.
EventuaUy the time came for this Brother to open his own office. Many of his clients,

mortal lUe.

This aroused my curiosity, and I asked which others

He refiected a moment. "Abraham Lincoln, certain

A Day With WilHam Howard
Taft, Beta 1878
In 1915, whUe I was a Junior at the University of
Wisconsin, Brother Taft, then Chief Justice of the
United States Supreme Court, came to Madison to
give a series of talks. On learning of his presence in
Madison, the Rho Chapter invited him to attend a
reception at the Chapter House. I was selected as
Chairman of the Reception Committee. I was elated,
when I contacted him at the Park Hotel, to find that
he accepted gladly our invitation. This did not sur
prise me, as he was always a loyal Psi U and devoted
considerable time to the Fratemity.
I arranged to pick him up after his last address at
the Old Armory Building. All through his talk I sat
nervously tiying to decide how I would approach such
a distinguished person! After he completed his talk
and came down from the dais, he was surrounded by
students, who asked him questions about current
events. I waited patiently until I thought it would be
an opportune time to approach him. A girl reporter for
The Cardinal, the student newspaper, had just asked
him what he thought about Women's Suffrage. Think
ing this might be an appropriate time to intervene, as
he obviously had no desire to answer the question, I
stepped forward and said, "Brother Taft, I have come
to take you to the Psi U House." He quickly replied,
"Let's go." Thereupon he put his arm around me, the
crowd cleared a path for us, and I walked proudly
with him to the open Packard, which we had rented
complete with chauffeur.
We drove around the campus, and when we arrived
at the House, in trying to squeeze his large torso
through the door of the car, his pocket caught on the
handle, and the stitches were ripped out. Naturally I
was very embarrassed and suggested, "While you are
here, I wiU send the coat out and have a tailor repair
it." He responded, "Young fellow, think notiiing of it.
My wffe brought her sewing bag with her, and she
will take care of it when I get back to the hotel." It
was such a down-to-earth expression from a great
man, and so typical of him, that it set me completely
at ease. From then on I was just as comfortable with
him as if I had known him all my life.
Tlie boys queued up in a reception hne to be in
tioduced to our famous Brother. When Gil Blake, Rho
'18, was intioduced to the former President of the
United States, he commented, "Brother Taft, I had the
honor of riding in the Black Horse Troop of Culver
Military Academy during your Inaugural in Wash
ington." The Chief Justice, in his humorous way, re
plied, "Oh, I remember you!" This, of course, was
obviously an exaggeration, as Gil was only one of
many in that group.
When we retumed Brother Taft to the hotel, I
thanked him for taking time from his busy schedule to
honor us with a visit to the House. He answered,
"Frankly, I enjoyed this occasion more than anything
else I have done during my visit to Madison."
This experience convinced me more than ever of the
wonderful Fratemity that Psi Upsilon is. When men
like Brother Taft, after attaining such statiire and
eminence, still maintain their allegiance to their col
lege fraternity, it must hold a rich meaning indeed.
Samuel C. Vail, Rho '16

Mrs. Corinne Avery, Epsilon Omega Cook
On January 16, 1975 Corinne Avery, a
very special
friend of the Epsilon Omega Chapter, died. For eigh
teen years until her retirement in 1968, Mrs. Avery
was the cook and honorary housemother for the
Northwestern Psi U's.
Corinne was as famous for her love of the Brothers
as she was for her fried chicken and apple pie. Once
each year she would prepare a prime rib feast for the
entire Chapter and their dates at her own
expense.
In February, 1970 Corinne and her late husband,
Luther Avery, returned to the Epsilon Omega to cele
brate the annual Epsilon Omega Founders' Day, held
that year in their honor.
A memorial service for Mrs. Avery was conducted
at Mount Zion Baptist Church in Evanston on
January
19. Several Brothers and their wives were in attend
ance. Brother Tom McSloy '71 delivered a short
eulogy, remembering Corinne's love and service for
"ber boys." Psi Upsilon has lost a great lady.
